On a label full of weirdos, outliers, mavericks and freaks, clandestine Greek anomaly Aeson Zervas is Heat Crimes’ OG wildcard, landing a debut album a couple of years ago that sounded like The Caretaker channeling crates of rebetika, and now returning with this deeply elusive new LP of plasmic synths that unfolds in ways that will leave you with a proper motion sickness of time travel. Aye, it’s a special one.

After lighting up 2024 with blink ’n miss LP & tape drops, Aeson Zervas’s 3rd instalment dips into a perpetual night world of cobwebbed keyboard melodies and flame flicker incantations designed to score your next regression session. As ever, the label and artist remain tight-lipped about pretty much everything, but the vibe is self-evidently clammy and febrile thru a dozen parts familiar to both preceding drops, woven between pillars of inspiration in lemniscate loops and free flowing rhythmelodic arrangements that bind his ideas to bezonked minds.

The Mesolonghi-based enigma continues to prove a master of hypnosis and a conduit for ancient spirits seeping into the modern world, luring susceptible minds to states of bliss and dread, but not without that sense of romance that also lit up his prior releases. Once again feeling the same pull of past worlds as The Caretaker, only slanted to microtonal scales, his mix of lopped-off and extended melodies tell arcane stories still salient to contemporary imaginations able to tune in.

Activating with a section of meditative, almost no-wave strafing discord, themes of shimmering exotica slide into backyard ritualism, with a lilting marimba sounding like it escaped a Martin Denny side before bleeding into a Giallo-esque wheeze, thru port and island-hopping rebetika, and properly haunting passages of midnight sacred music swarmed by cicadas. The 6th (Χωρίς τίτλο 23) part of needling Italianate arps and screeches is particularly affective, as is the plugged-in folkdance sputter of the 8th (Χωρίς τίτλο 25), and a final couplet coming off like Muslimgauze with a thing for sleazy horror, not dub.

Basically, whatever this label serve, lap it up while you can.

Lovers of ZudRangMa, Khruangbin, and even the White Lotus 3 soundtrack will be enchanted with Korlakang’s chiming, low-slung meld of ’70s psych pop and Luk Thung from the quieter side of Bangkok...

“Korlakang are four young friends from Thonburi, the quieter, canal-laced western bank of Bangkok, where temple bells and river rhythms shape everyday life. Formed from a bond that stretches back to high school hallways and shared university years, the band came together with a sound rooted in Thai traditional music and the warm haze of psychedelic rock.

Their debut 7-inch, Samong Sai, is that rare thing: a record that seems to arrive already aged, carrying the grain and warmth of a forgotten 70s pressing. It seeps in slowly, sweet and chill, like sound faintly coming through a neighbour's window. The kind of music that makes you stop what you're doing just to hear a little more of.”

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.

items.body:
Nueen follows production for Iceboy Violet and a string of releases for Quiet Time Tapes, Good Morning Tapes and Balmat, with a sprawling new album for 3XL, an ambient drill epic featuring guest spots from Dawuna, Space Afrika, Loraine James, Xzavier Stone and RenzNiro.

Everything clicked into place for Nacho Pezzati when he turned the humid soundscapes of his early releases into distorted beds for Iceboy Violet's casual free associations on the Hyperdub-released ‘You Said You'd Hold My Hand Through the Fire' back in 2024. He retains the same energy on 'Swerved', working alongside a team of vocalists and collaborators to locate a sweetspot between rap, dub and ambient vistas. His methodology is laid bare on 'Searchtiers', obscuring its UK drill-style sliding bass with weightless synths and gaseous FX, upping the ante when vocalist and producer Xzavier Stone jumps on the mic on 'Nowhere Near A Section'. The addition of proper hooks, adlibs and rhymes - "let it burn like Usher Raymond" - makes the production hit that much harder, not just referencing radio rap and R&B but challenging the paradigm. Fittingly, Loraine James, who early on inhabited similar zones, lends her voice to the grimy 'Atmosphere is my Style', whispering over Pezzati's hair metal samples and booming 808 Mafia-style basses. 

Manny's own RenzNiro checks in on 'Impls', rhyming over one of Nueen's most decisive beats, all clipped snares, gong samples and tweaked bass. And Space Afrika turn up with an assist on the low-slung highlight 'Shm', a smoove and sensual D'Angelo-style soul banger with none other than Dawuna on the mic. Dawuna returns on 'Matrix', splitting duties with Xzavier Stone who provides an impressive '00s post-jiggy hook and Pezzati's vision materialises. The haze of half-remembered bites of cloud rap, pop and club rap represents a post-P2P hauntology that's global, not really localised. And connecting with Space Africa again on the closing track 'I Guess', he travels beyond the boundaries of the album itself, lavishing SA's orchestral cries with fuzzy synths and swirling vocals.

Mike Paradinas picks 18 scuzzy examples of Nondi_’s wistful take on footwork, ambient noise, and dub techno as an addendum to a strong eponymous 2nd album, nodding to precedents from Actress, AFX, µ-Ziq...

"Following her acclaimed 2023 release Flood City Trax, a dreamy, lo-fi take on footwork inspired by the crumbling rust-belt city she calls home, Nondi returns to Planet Mu with her second self-titled album, Nondi…

While Nondi… retains some of the hazy, nostalgic atmosphere of Flood City Trax, it pushes her sound in bold new directions. “I made this album to capture the sense of freedom I used to get from music when I was first discovering it all,” Nondi says. “It’s meant to be cute, fun, kinda weird and emotional — but most of all, it’s a presentation of some of the prettiest tracks I’ve made.” Though she hasn’t really experienced club culture where she lives, her impressionistic productions evoke the surreal, lingering sounds of a night out — the melodic haze that hums in your ears as you drift off to sleep. Lo-fi and melodic, yet fluid and free, her music carries a sense of flight and intuitive logic. Nondi’s influences range widely — Actress, Aphex Twin, footwork, and the stranger edges of dub techno are all felt, yet she hallucinates them through her own weathered, dreamlike lens. Her tracks often build from clashing loops that evolve and transform organically, or from familiar genre elements reshaped by her instinct for misty, heart-wrenching melody. Nondi… is a uniquely moving and exploratory album that expands her sonic world even further. Lo-fi yet luminous, playful yet profound."

Peak Oil mooch in our back yard again with a strong album from YOUTH & Shotta Tapes alum Leo - the latest in their line of UK mutants (Paperclip Minimiser, Low End Activist, Wrecked Lightship) and a definitive statement of classic uk dub-as-method in electroid 2-step and crooked dembow forms.

A whirring cog in the Manchester machine, Leo has spent the 2020s rent in brooding negative space. His 4th album, ‘Cicada Burnt’ emerges in six segments that harness his drummer’s sleight of hand and feel for textured production on structures that teem with hi-tech sound design, insectoid detail and weathered pressure systems. No doubt it’s his most impressive artistic statement thus far, straddling key, extramusical reference points nabbed from his roots in Pennine Oldham landscapes and work strafing the industrial city downhill, and in that sense comparable with the Skam/NMB nexus or DDS’ cloud-seeding rufige.

Under the ochre artwork of Sean Clarke, who does Leo’s live visuals, the album smoulders with a dusky light and particulates in the air, conjuring immersive environmental settings and subtle tensions between the anticipatory rhythms and dread gloom. We can hear coruscating echoes of Paperclip Minimiser’s pendulous metric intricacy via Autechre in ‘Qwershape’, and his adroit percussive instincts on the tight electro-rolls of a ‘Jetti’ reminding us of Gescom's Cybotron-sampling classic 'Puzl', as well as low key Skam legend Mike Williamson - the guy behind that sick Grace Jones edit on Mask 400. His feel for syncopated nuance is zipped tightest in the grimy dembow of ‘Descant’, and likewise a weightless ‘Spirit Level (Prescript)’ demonstrating patiently poised, heightened proprioceptions, held in balance with the tendon-twitching steppas closer ‘Spirit Level’.

items.body:
Good Morning Tapes with a fully sick digital steppas session from DJ and rave shotter Carl Luis of the Merger soundsystem - a big look FFO Blazer Sound System, G Version III, and Raime’s ‘Can You Repeat That Please?’ mixtape.

With a steady hand on the FX, Carl Luis treats the dance to over an hour of militant, tuffest pressure and more spangled gems in a crucial style of ’80s & ‘90s JA x UK sound system weaponry. It’s brimming over with the sort of propulsive, trudging and flying steppas that’s lit dances from Brixton to Chapeltown, Hulme to Berlin for the last 40 years, dancing at the square root of so much music we all love - from early bleep ’n bass to jungle, dub techno, broken beat and dubstep - in a very particular style and pattern. 

Plastic horn pomp ramps with seismic subby tremors and sizzling drum machines in myriad formations, strafing from a late ‘80s zinger, shades away from darkest new beat monk chants, thru 8-bit cone quakers and knees-ups jogged with judicious digits on the dial, to a notable balmier, woozier B-side where his feel for atmospheric levity and hypnotic velocity really comes into play.

How much patience you'll have for this one depends on your interest in Zelda, no doubt. Because from the opening seconds of the 15-minute 'Overworld Suite', it's clear that 'The Z Suites' is Zelda first. The trio of Liberski, bassist Janos Bruneel and drummer Diogo Alexandre clearly love the source material, trekking through all the important moments from 'Ocarina of Time', 'Link's Awakening', 'A Link to the Past' and the original game that started it all. But we have to wonder whether there would ever be a moment to reach for this rather than play Kondō's timeless originals.

Inspired by Shigeru Miyamoto's iconic 'The Legend of Zelda' games, cellist and composer Patrick Belaga imagines his latest full-length as a map of fantastical locations, using the language of 20th century minimalism and Coil's unsettling soundscapes to provoke exploration rather than resolution.

When you cite video games as a reference, you can guarantee that almost anyone reading will immediately bring to mind their favorite cues: the low-bitrate Russian folk variations of 'Tetris' or the ubiquitous 'Super Mario Bros' theme. Unexpectedly, these aren't the reference points Belaga makes on 'Solar Calf'. Rather, his interest is in a game's playability, how the meticulously programmed environments allow players to navigate the story in their own way, moving from area to area and sometimes avoiding the core narrative altogether. The concept provided him with a way of swerving the expectation to produce an album that reads beginning to end like a book or a movie and approach it like a game designer instead, considering non-linear listening.

Even the sounds are designed to mimic the aesthetics of a game, not really the clusters of phrases and SFX featured in the background music. As you might expect if you've heard Belaga's previous material, his PAN debut 'Blutt' or his collaboration with Asma Maroof and Tapiwa Svosve 'The Sport of Love', he plays a selection of instruments, but mixes up these sounds with samples, even re-sampling his playing to muddy the picture even more. He's eager to make his landscape as confusing as it is inviting and the compositions themselves, stuttering Reich-ian phrases and Glass-style repetitions that give just a casual glance to Koji Kondo's 'Ocarina of Time' OST, continue the concept, playing like interlocking puzzles that work best shuffled, replayed and engaged with differently each time.

Bewitching, sound sensitive and psychedelic experiments from LA’s Celia Hollander ($3.33), landing somewhere between Carl Stone and Laurel Halo...

“Celia Hollander works with digital audio as a medium to intuitively form temporal experiences. Each song in Recent Futures aspires towards a different type of temporal movement: a swing between the recent past and near future, an accelerating present, a temporal eddy, a juxtaposition between massive and microscopic durations, a flowing momentum and a preserved stillness. An assemblage of field recordings drenched, sampled, tumbled, stretched, diced, dyed, layered and reversed, Recent Futures yields varying terrains of the abstracted mundane, a magical realism of audio. 

Celia Hollander is an LA based composer and artist working with audio, scores, performance, installation and text. Her work critically engages ways that audio and the act of listening can shape temporal perception, generate narratives, question cultural infrastructures and cultivate social connection. Her work has been performed or installed in venues and institutions including MOCA, The Getty, Kunsthalle Basel, Cirrus Gallery LA, Human Resources LA and Zebulon, LA and she is a resident dj on Dublab Radio.”

items.body:
Weird America instigator and survivor Sir Richard Bishop expands his hillbilly series with an album of raw, unplugged "moonshine-drunk" sex jams... really.

Last year, Bishop reminded us that the so-called "American Primitive" genre, or at least the legion of John Fahey-inspired guitarists who drew on ragas and American folk music with equal amounts of zeal, were being "way too safe". His prescription was an unrefined, crude style that went back to real basics; gone was the pomp and circumstances of the bourgeois avant-garde and in walked Schrödinger's hillbilly - an avatar he embodied on the pretty self-explanatory 'Hillbilly Ragas'. And he goes a step further into polite societal discomfort on 'Hillbilly Erotica', picking up where its predecessor left off but heading towards the bedroom, boldly asserting that contemporary experimental folk music doesn't need to be sexless.

Fittingly, his titles circle the same territory, approaching erotica not from a sanitised vantage point but from the South with its funk and humidity. The rush of 'Lick Skillet' draws us in and Bishop's already on top form, showing that he doesn't need any embellishment at all to do his thing. And by 'Finger, Tennessee', he's in a genuinely romantic mood, creating a fingerstyle version of what might as well be the outro to a romantic comedy. Thankfully, we're in more familiarly raga-inspired territory on 'Sweet Lips Spiritual' and that's where Bishop really shines, spotlighting the sensuality of a musical form that has its roots in midnight performances by candlelight. If there's a weirder record of late-night gear this year, we'll be surprised.

‘Kissa’ quietly diverges from 48208 World’s usual tuff knocks for a sublime, 8-part album swanning from dreamy, floating vignettes to bittersweet beatdown house nuanced with a mix of Japanese and Detroit late night je ne sais quoi. Tokyo’s clandestine back street jazz listening bars prompt Anthony “Mathias” R. to play it down, in-the-pocket, in procession from the Radiophonic siren of ‘Moonlit Steep’, thru the echoes of Neil Ollivierra’s The Detroit Escalator Company on ‘Kissa’, or C2-esque arp flutters in ‘Velvet Oolong’. He coaxes a certain, tangy tone from his kit on ‘Yuza Drift’ like some imaginary Susumu Yokota meets Howard Thomas joint, and winks at Japanese ambient electronics in ‘Sakura Steam’, saving a real beatdown pearl for those willing to dive deeper in ‘Amber Infusion’.

In physical stature and imaginative scope, Luc Ferrari’s 10 x CD / 11 Hour selection for INA GRM’s series presents a poetic building block of C.20th electronic music from the founding director of the GRM in 1958, presenting a unique art history spanning six decades of ingenious, beguiling soundcraft.

Part of a legendary series including titles by concrète pioneers Pierre Schaefer & Pierre Henry, plus weighty surveys of Bernrad Parmegiani, Éliane Radigue and François Bayle, this lavish boxset of Luc Ferrari’s work is a masterclass exploration of avant garde form and function that charts experimental music’s research and development during a radical phase. While even the notion of such a large storage device for sound was unimaginable when Ferrari began making his cut-up musical collages and sound poetry in the ‘50s, his ‘L’Œuvre Électronique’ covers the progression of musical technology and thought from its most laboriously executed origins, working with tape and raw blocks of sound, to the grander digital staging of his ‘90s and early ‘00s radio plays, plotted for multiple voices and spatialised landscapes. 

Collected, this set forms an incredible deep dive into art-music history where the materiality of sound is questioned and reconsidered in relief of its musical connotations, creating in the process a peerless body of work that better approximates the texture of dreams or the audness of waking life than any song, and has long informed the approach to sound organisation by a host of progressive artists, effectively bridging the conceptual precedents of Varèse and Cage and the contemporary futures projected by Lee Gamble or Valerio Tricoli.

The 98 tracks from 31 releases, clocking up just over 10 hours of recordings, delineate across decades following Ferrari’s studies with Messaien and Honegger in the mid ‘50s, and a period of illness that made him better acquainted with the radio receiver, and pioneers such as Schöneberg and Webern, to his co-founding of the Groupe de Recherches Musicales with Schaeffer and François-Bernard Mâche in 1958, and thru his landmark transformation of field recordings made on a Yugoslavian beach, and the ravishing abstractions of later electronic works. 

Until his passing, aged 76 in Arezzo, Italy, Ferrari remained ceaselessly active both in his own practice and teaching, and was revered as the poet of musique concrète. He bought a particularly gallic purview to the paradigm, especially when considered against the more hard-nosed academic pursuits of his peers, making singular use of vocals as an elusive or sometimes literal presence in his works in a way that others didn’t, and as such his works all hare a certain liminal quality that appears richly seductive to fans of fantasy storytelling as much as psychedelic soundtracks and sound as dreamfood imagery.

The classic 12 disc Parmegiani Box Set finally given a reissue by INA GRM, covering the majority of Parmegiani's musique concrète output recorded between 1964 and 2007. Is there a more important, influential, totemic single-artist collection in all of electronic music?

The Wire magazine described it as a "bargain price treasure chest....containing worlds of inexhaustible spaciousness and strangeness" and, indeed, listening through just some of the 12 cd's included you find yourself drawn into a multi-faceted world full of timeless treasure.

Parmegiani was mentored by the founding father of Musique Concrète, Pierre Schaeffer, who made use of technological advances that gave the world magnetic tape and microphones to pioneer a method taking everyday noise and transforming them into unrecognisable sounds, a style that became known as Acousmatic music. 

Parmegiani would go on to make use of these Acousmatic techniques in creating a body of work which is not only one of the most significant of the 20th century, but also hugely influential on a whole host of musical pioneers that would follow in his wake, with Christian Fennesz, Aphex Twin, Kode9 and Jim O'Rourke being notable disciples in the contemporary field. 

It’s hard to comprehend let alone articulate the immersive and often woozy effect of these recordings, ranging from eerie cut-out tape loops through to popular music plunderphonics and proto-distilled-dub that's impossible to absorb in one sitting. In short, L’Œuvre Musicale is one of the most impressive and important collections of electronic music you'll likely ever hear, but also one of the most rewarding.

"In a world currently defined by unrest, uncertainty, and cultural fracture, acclaimed saxophonist, composer, and bandleader Isaiah Collier returns with Joy, a 5-track EP that reframes one of humanity’s most nuanced emotions both as a devotional grounding and political act. 

Collier’s deeply personal compositions present joy as an act that isn’t rooted in escapism or abstraction, but rather, as something hard-won rooted in lived experience, shaped by transformation, and sustained through connection. Throughout the album’s five compositions, Collier positions joy as a guiding light during challenging times, an expression of challenging yourself to utilize your gifts, an affirmation of love and discovery, and as an affirmative source of reassurance."

Codeine, Elliott Smith and Cancer House fiends will be in their element with the bittersweet slowcore and swoon of Goldenstar’s debut, a fine new addition to the Montreal scene, fixed up with engineering/mix/master by Francis Latreille (Priori and Patrick Holland (Project Pablo).

"goldenstar is a band from Montreal. Chamber Music is their EP. It’s out on OST. It takes them to the altar of a relatively new but already widely resonant North American musical canon: it’s a self-avowed slowcore record, a term that conjures intimacy, slow-glowing guitars, and ride cymbals that bathe and shimmer. It’s a term fraught with the legacy of universally beloved forebears like Duster, Bedhead, Codeine, et al. A pantheon of sorts. Slowcore carries weight. But this is no retread. Chamber Music’s palette is recognisable, but reconstituted through the idiosyncrasies of its songwriting: the creeping unease on opener ‘Forget’ and the sleepwalking lamentation of ‘Spinning Out’, songs whose warmth are framed by an ever-present anxiety that ebbs and bobs like lantern light on ocean water.

‘Thread’ unspools a kind of shaky optimism, undercutting every swell of hope with a chord change that eases the realisation of its falseness. The downcast note it ends on is carried through to the EP’s second half, which brings the pace down to a hypnotic sway. ‘Belemen’ and ‘April 3’ are scenic views through tired, dark-circled eyes, twinges of memories felt but elusive, meaning that recedes further every time it’s recalled. Instrumental closer ‘I Blink and See Nothing’ concludes numbly, spiralling downwards like a stomach butterfly turned to a moth. These are songs that speak to stillness and solitude and slow-burning pangs of regret: words unheard and half-thoughts left unspoken, a creeping sense that taking your own advice will only ever reveal the meaning it lacks. It’s about hollowness, it’s music that constructs a chamber in the familiar surroundings of a well-worn void. Welcome down."

aloisius's enigmatic life is beautiful label/collective/ fully establishes its lore on this colossal compilation: 39 tracks of whimsical pop, edgy improv, freewheeling poetry, noise, dusty psych, abstract hip-hop, folk and saccharine soul from artists you'll know and a fair few you won't. Featuring Bianca Scout, VOICE ACTOR, James Massiah, Kenichi Iwasa, THE NARRATOR, Isaiah Hull and many, many more.

If you've spent any amount of time orbiting Cafe Oto, streaming NTS or even browsing these pages, you'll surely have interfaced with life is beautiful, even by accident. The self-styled "gesamtkunstwerk" was established by the mysterious aloisius in 2022 initially as a radio show, before he decided to complicate things with a collective, a series of live performances and a record label a year later. And after booking artists like Klein, Lauren Duffus, YHWH Nailgun, John Glacier and DJ Spanish Fly, and releasing genuinely off-kilter records from James Massiah, Pretty V and THE NARRATOR, life is beautiful comes correct with its first compilation - and it's good. We shouldn't have expected less from a label who dump their demos and experiments ("resources and inspiration") on a file exchange portal on their own site, but the set is remarkably generous, scraping together ideas, performances and fully-fledged tracks from  a host of their core members, regular collaborators and close associates. 

Fittingly, the set opens with tracks from each of the founders, who establish the label's core sound. NWAKKE begins with 'i need you in a positive way', a cloudy hypnagogic R&B marvel that juxtaposes her cool-headed vocal runs with melancholy drones, spy movie strings, tape-fucked field recordings and piano punctuations. Then the mic's handed to Amber Joy, aka THE NARRATOR, who also works as the label's artistic director; on 'SUDDENLY', she follows spring's beguiling 'RADIOWEAVER' with another skittish post-everything collage that chops 'n pastes cheap synth vamps, molasses-slow breaks and choral vocals into a dreamy modern hymn. And aloisus' 'you are god' runs out of its stuck groove as if it's from the very same thought, blurring gospel moans across Prince-like drum machine loops and EZ-listening piano phrases. Bianca Scout hands us a taster of her collaborative project with London's Cajm on the hypnotic 'Welcome to Hello' , while poet Isaiah Hull teams up with y+Your for the wonked 'vampire money'.

Japser Maurice, aka jaso, turns in a short, guitar-led theme and cellist abi asisa shifts the set into a completely different direction on 'calling', complimenting her eerie dissonances with clipped, decelerated beats. Basically there's a whole record of music from the crew before 'veneration...' has begun in earnest, and it only gets better from here, running through aesthetic experiments from multi-instrumentalist Kenichi Iwasa, self-styled "beat wizard" psychedelic ensemble. (who's one half of Brum's Everything is Psychedelic with Tony Bontana) and Thom Dehli before we reach the compilation's crown jewel, a 21-minute live performance from okk70 ensemble. We can't tell you exactly who's playing, but it's worth the price of entry alone, a squirming slo-mo jazz side that gets to the roots of the life is beautiful sound.

Elsewhere there's a chewably eccentric solo moment from Bianca Scout ('superscribe 24'), a phenomenally moody collaboration between VOICE ACTOR and aloisius ('24'), a spirited, lo-fi transmission from London's josiane pozi and a deeper than deep jam from orchestra379, aloisius' "collective improvisation project" that's featured artists like Ben Vince, Kenichi Iwasa and abi asisa. Honestly there's so much more than we can even readily dive into - label comps are so often a slog but this one's stuffed to the gills with genuinely creative experimentation from some of the London scene's most beguiling outsiders.

items.body:
After the dissolution of his wave-making duo project Ameli Paul, Berlin based musician and producer Paul Valentin aims to venture down new roads and finds help from illustrious folks like Liv Lisa Fries, DJ Koze, Thomass Jackson and Philipp Fein along the way.

"Valentin’s debut EP on Feines Tier marks his first solo release in 10 years and is a colourful journey through sonic worlds and emotions in the continuous search for his own sound.

Opener ELVAU is a collaboration with actor Liv Lisa Fries built around their intimate voice recordings which are woven delicately into a dreamy web of shimmering synths atop pulsating break beats that would make Bicep proud. For his remix, His Kosiness, the Tripsitter Himself also known as DJ Koze follows the breakbeat path further down, gleefully taking all sorts of wonky and fun diversions on the way, which makes one hope that the ride never ends.

Follow-up tune MALFUNCTION is a more straightforward affair with its rolling synth arps and is - in Valentin’s own words - “about personal failure, dissolution, and the distortion of the self“. Equally dark under- and overtones are throwing shades over WHATTHE!, dealing with anger and transformations, resulting in a banger for the heavier moments on the dancefloor or the mind between your headphones. The EP closes on a more hopeful note with LISTEN, which stands for „everything that could be, if we listened to each other“. And it’s never a bad idea to listen to chirping 303 basslines, especially when paired with melancholic synth pads and weird vocal samples, as is the case here. The rework of Thomass Jackson and FT-head honcho Philipp Fein feels beautifully anachronistic with its reduced tempo and could have been something Andrew Weatherall would have played when he was still playing our earthly dancefloors."

items.body:
Smouldering and aching in all the right places, Dawuna's latest mixtape is a muted hypnagogic R&B tour de force, pieced together while recovering from a traumatic head injury and conveying all the fragile, dizzy and ineffable beauty imaginable. Trust, it’s next-level gear tipped FFO D’Angelo, Prince, Niecy Blues, Soulquarians, Rodney Jerkins.

‘African Family Laptop Musick’ is Ian Mugerwa’s 4th dispatch as Dawuna since 2020’s still unfathomable ‘Glass Lit Dream’, an album that we called "the debut of the century thus far" and which has still, somehow, evaded any kind of meaningful crossover despite triggering total joy and bewilderment every single time we play it to the uninitiated. Since that album, and shortly after a relocation to Baltimore, Mugerwa was involved in a car accident that triggered a period of hospitalisation and amnesia. 'African Family Laptop Music' emerges from that difficult period; recorded and pieced together while still in recovery. He doesn't remember much about the project at this point, just small flashes, but it's easily the most personal, touching material he's shared to date. 

Mugerwa calls the compositions simple, but it’s the kind of simple many have spent a lifetime trying to engineer. On opener 'I am a woman too', daring lo-fi sound design lends texture to multi-tracked vocal harmonies and a beat rapped on a table with knuckles and finger clicks, before tuning in to a chat between elders on ‘Obulesi’, that he laments in the bloozy ache of the incredible ‘Family Trauma Drama’. Lashed to a celestial vocal performance, he fleshes out the arrangement with downsampled waltzing hats and a single snare hit with synths that sound like they've been lifted from a mid-'80s Sierra adventure game, before being filtered out to a low hum. There's a quiet virtuosity on show; it's lo-fi, with all the aesthetic hallmarks of some of the very best outsider gear, but Mugerwa builds on the foundations of 'Glass Lit Dream' and 'Naya' to provide an unmistakably Black ideation of hauntology. Approaching the very concept of memory from a unique vantage point, he muddles dreams and impressions, sorting through the canon (think 'Songs in the Key of Life', 'Sign O' the Times', 'Baduizm', 'Brown Sugar' and 'Full Moon' just for starters) as it vanishes from view. 

What makes the record hit even harder is that Mugerwa collages the more “proper” songs with skits and interludes that help map the narrative, taping conversations with his family and abstracting them with disorientating glitches, synths and FX. ‘Pressure’ pushes deep on a bittersweet bruise with lyrics about “the pain on your brain making fun of you”, set to the heaviest smudge of bass and organ recalling Angel Bat Dawid’s ‘The Oracle’, whilst the latter stages reveal precious gems in the harpsichord sway of ‘Bipolar Memory’,thru the lip-biting downswang and helium-voiced Camille vibes of ‘Grabba Boy Problem’ and a poignant sign-off addressed to his father - not sure if that’s his dad or him upstairs - in a delicate prayer ‘Undo This Damage,’ which once over, is bound to make you rake back over all Dawuna’s gear to date. 

"This is the last lil offering from a personal side of myself before I give y'all something big," he assures cryptically. "Enjoy."

Incredible, really.

items.body:
Remastered and reissued for its 20th anniversary, ELEH's viscerally austere debut album, made using analog synths, tube oscillators and guitars, is still just as remarkably heavy as it was way back when.

There are countless ELEH albums to choose from at this stage, but the very first, released way back in 2006, still holds a special place in our hearts. We didn't know what to expect back then; Important boss Jon Brien had started the project in 1999 and kept it anonymous at first, wanting to keep the project pure - all about sound, not about any kind of identity. And it's hard to express just how hard it hit back then, released in the middle of the hipster era as pop tangled with folk and underground bucked under the weight of late-stage post-rock. Brien was pulling from a different frame of reference, waving to the mystickal minimalism of La Monte Young and 'Time Machines'-era Coil urging listeners to tune in as deeply as they might while gripped to one of Pauline Oliveros' classic sides. 

This particular album was the first in a trilogy, each dedicated to one of Brien's foundational heroes: Young, Charlemagne Palestine and Oliveros, respectively. But the ingredients remained largely the same; Brien used his oscillators and synths in a manner that completely avoided the showiness that began to weigh down the scene (and prop up a lucrative second-hand marketplace). Concerned with tone above all, he became central to a kind of analog purity that's still a joy to absorb, preserving the tones that make the music so physically affecting. Opening side 'In the Ear of the Gods' might start simply enough, with a low-end drone that's ruptured by a pulsing rhythm, but by the back half, it's completely driven by its unsettling psychoacoustic effects - the warbling, beating resonances, whistling high-end frequencies and booming subs.

On the flip, Brien writes for "guitars & 4 oscillators", stacking his tones into a droning wall of sound that barely moves unless you focus carefully. And it's as heavy as anything O'Malley has gotten his hands into.

Crazy find from Death Is Not The End, shining a light on proto-everything works from "multi-media theater" pioneer Alwin Nikolais, 1966-1989, a missing link connecting classic concrète, Oramics and Wally Badarou’s 4th world jams thru 21 energetic and prophetic early electronic experiments that redrew the synthesizer's boundaries, accompanying his inventive avant-garde dance productions.

The owner of the very first Moog synthesizer, Nikolais is one of electronic music's unsung heroes, a choreographer, dancer and composer who understood the revolutionary potential of electronic music long before most of his peers. Using his Moog and a notoriously complicated Synclavier system, he composed the majority of the music to his productions himself, having had an early training on the piano and organ, moonlighting as a silent film musician. His interest in dance had been triggered by an obsession with percussion and for his earliest dance pieces he imagined the dancers banging on car parts and children's toys, creating their own live score. But the more he learned about tape music, the more Nikolais became convinced that he could control his own unique sound. He assembled a library of abstract loops and hits, composing 11 scores between 1956 and 1962 in the musique concrète mode, but was drawn to electronic sounds when his assistant James Seawright provided him with an archive of synthesizer bleeps and drones recorded at the Columbia-Princeton Center for Electronic Music.

It was Seawright who told Nikolais about Robert Moog,and convinced him to confront the young engineer at an electronics expo in New York. And after trying Moog's prototype and sharing his ideas, Nikolais used his Guggenheim Fellowship money to purchase the first Moog - a legendary synth that's now displayed in Ann Arbor's Museum of Musical Instruments. It's that instrument we can hear in all its glory on the earliest pieces included on the anthology, most prominently on the 1966 composition 'Chimera: Dance I'. Extraordinarily, Nikolais doesn't appear to be motivated by the Moog's ability to shadow other instruments, instead intrigued by its rhythmic capabilities, generating dissonant tones, scraped distortions and whirring resonances that he assembles into loping movements. And a decade later, he's still coaxing genuinely befuddling sounds from the Moog, making it shriek Banshee-like on 'Tribe: Dance' and duck beneath the earth's mantle on 'Styx: Excerpt'.

In the late '70s however, Nikolais' attention turned towards the New England Digital Corporation's Synclavier, a digital synthesizer and (later at least) sampling workstation controlled by an early computer that foreshadowed the next couple of decades of electronic music. Ever the early adopter, Nikolais used this system to write his next slew of scores, harnessing the notoriously complex FM additive synth architecture and finding his predictably idiosyncratic sweet spot. On 1980's 'Mechanical Organ: Dance II', for example, Nikolais plays the Synclavier's uncanny tones off bone-rattling live percussion sounds and 'Pierrot: Dance II' uses the early sampler technology to shadow the drums with pitchy vocalizations. The most startling thing about the set is that we haven't heard it before - really, it's worth a look just for the almost 10-minute deployment of ring modulated tones, FM harps, analog wubs and corroded samples that concludes the set, an excerpt of Nikolais' batshit score for 1985's 'Crucible'.

Dimensional percussives with gelatinous sonics blend into a blanket of ambience composed of vibrational pools of VHS static. Like an audio journal sourced from his surroundings, Loose Leaf is the personification of the northwest rainy season filtered through a dusty Tascam.”

Oh man this is almost too much - just wall to wall genius in action courtesy of Floating Points & Eliot Bernard's Melodies International label -  spotlightling fire in the crown of Mad Professor’s pivotal London Lovers Rock and dub stable, Ariwa Sounds: from an immense monk-steppa ‘Non Violence Dub’ ft. Horace Andy, thru the Motown soul-infused Lovers of Davina Stone on 'Silly Wasn’t I’, to a Kofi gem recently found on Moin’s street-soul/digidub mix, the ruffneck charge of Mafia & Fluxy ‘6 Million Dub’, early Wild Bunch styles on Aisha’s ‘Can You Feel It’, and deadly ‘Liberated Woman’ voiced by Ranking Ann. All killer no filler!

“In 1979, Neil Fraser (artistically known as Mad Professor) founded Ariwa Sounds, the longest-serving and one of the most influential independently owned Reggae studios and record labels in the UK. From humble beginnings set up in the front room of Neil's home in South London recording on 4-track and homemade equipment, Ariwa would go on to record and release over 300 albums including works from some of the most impactful and storied artists of their time in the genres of Reggae, Dub, and Lovers Rock

Whilst our previous release in collaboration with Ariwa captured the label's early sound, a shared performance with Neil in Osaka and regular visits to his South London studio inspired us to assemble this 15-track compilation, showcasing the label's output across 45 years. Our release emphasizes some of the label's greatest vocalists: Johnny Clarke, Sandra Cross, Kofi, U Roy, Sister Nancy, Queen Omega, Aisha, Garnett Cross, Abel Miller, Horace Andy and more — presenting the Motown and Stax influences in the Lovers Rock, but also provides a glimpse into the dubbier and more experimental side of the label, showcasing Ariwa's commitment to quality but also their personality, philosophy and their humour. Love songs, break-up songs, socially engaged songs, dub experimentations — this compilation is not a "best of" Ariwa but a diverse and honest celebration of the label through the lens of Melodies International.”

items.body:
Relocating from Dean Spunt's PPM imprint to Kranky, Cate Kennan embraces the recent past on 'Shadows', dreaming up a soundtrack to her Los Angeles surroundings by isolating gentle psych-folk memories and West Coast ambient frills compiling her own set of library-ready cues.

There's a charming glow to 'Shadows' that makes you question its title. The album was written when Kennan returned to the LA neighborhood she'd grown up in and realised how much it had changed as she'd been away. It's a record that deals with the passing of time head-on and does so by playing with our concept of nostalgia, or the sounds we most readily associate with it. That means tape-recorded guitars, mellotrons, library-style FX, washy analog synths, Raymond Scott-style rhythms and Trish Keenan-style vocals. And although there's a feeling that the past is raining down on us as 'Shadows' takes shape, Kennan's vignettes are never mawkish.

On the title track, she buries her voice in white noise, dipping it just beneath her guitar strums and the wheezing organ. And as the album moves forward, so does her ambition; on 'Devil's Hour', xenharmonic synth bleeps and kosmische beatscapes help propel her psychedelic reflections and on the lengthy 'So Far Away', her folky strumming is snagged in an ambient synthscape that eventually takes hold completely. Gorgeous stuff.

items.body:
The entwined timelines of Bristol, Africa, and Peter Gabriel’s WOMAD festival and Real World label, manifest across eight previously unreleased, early ’80s jams by a mix of West African, Jamaican and Avon-based musicians, at best in the polyrhythmic groovers by Ben Baddoo International, and an unusual sort of proto-trip hop fusion by Bhundu Boys frontman, Biggie Tembo, with Startled Insects, who would go on to key work with Massive Attack and Madonna...

“It’s more than a special moment when you discover music you’ve never heard (of) before or ever knew existed. 1982 was a critical spark for the development of wider (world) musical styles, both in Bristol and the UK at large. The central event from that year was the first WOMAD festival, held in the unlikely surroundings of the agricultural themed Bath and West Showground near Shepton Mallet in Somerset.

One common thread in Bristol to all of these discoveries was the Ekome Dance Company and most notably Artistic Director, Barrington ‘Barry’ Anderson. Barry had also recruited musicians from African countries such as Cameroon and Ghana, from Jamaica and others from the Bristol area. This was to form the Ekome Arts Band which would offer music with either a specific African or Caribbean focus.

This kickstarted a process and practice in the West Country city where musicians brought over from African countries would collaborate with those from the locality. It is those activities - a sound clash and culture clash, producing material of real depth - that constitute the three different combinations, along with one connection originating in London, that make up material on the first The Bristol Meets Africa Music Sound album, released on Bristol Archive Records.”

items.body:
The Durutti Column's first album in 16 years, 'Renascent' is a celestial lap of honor for Vini Reilly and his long-time collaborators Keir Stewart and Bruce Mitchell, recorded in Reilly’s Didsbury kitchen and held together by his signature echoed-out fretwork and the languid melancholia that's been in place since that milestone first LP. 

Reilly's a survivor. We've all heard the legend by now, the stories that used to travel from friend to friend in the Manchester scene's pubs and backrooms: That Reilly had knocked around with local gangs and lived on the street before he'd been taken in by Factory boss Tony Wilson in the late '70s, or that he'd been sectioned during the making of his first album. The truth, of course, is probably stranger; tormented by anxiety and depression, Reilly was always a difficult, vulnerable character - something that made his art infinitely fascinating to Wilson. So Factory Records became an outlet for Reilly's expressions; despite never capturing the attention of the mainstream, The Durutti Column became the label's house act - a band who'd become critical darlings long before they could make a living from their art. Indeed, at this stage, almost a half-century since the release of 'The Return of the The Durutti Column', the band is still respectably niche, despite having picked up steam in the last few years. They've got famous fans - including Frank Ocean, AG Cook and Blood Orange - but Reilly has never felt the need to write anything more universal. He does what he's always done: reflect his emotional reality, knowledge and spectrum of musical interests in shimmering fretwork that, at this stage, has influenced countless artists.

Although since the band's last proper album, 'A Paean to Wilson', Reilly has suffered three strokes, his distinct tone still shines through on 'Renascent'. Simply operating in a timeline of his own, Reilly’s uniquely inspirational style of classical, folk, and jazz guitar playing is typically vaulted to high Didsbury ceiling scale, floating on air where it meets Caoilfhionn Rose’s heat hazy cadence on ‘Agonistes’, and condenses into torch song jazz ballad ‘Sargasso Sea’, and ultimately elides Lucas Elliot’s plangent croon in closer ‘All They See is Fire’. You could be forgiven for mistaking a whole orchestra assembled in his kitchen on ‘For Friends Everywhere’ - a symphonic render of ‘For Our Belgian Friends’, masterfully weft with Sam Morris (French horn), John Ellis (keys), and Liz Rossi (violin) - but Reilly’s spirit is the guiding light throughout: drawing it down into almost Tricky-esque dream-pop/trip-hop on ‘Liars’, and adjacent to A.R. Kane on ‘Vapour In A Matchbox’, a rare moment to hear Reilly on his own, jamming into a distorted amplifier and letting the phrases coil into a fuzzy, transcendent wall of sound. It might as well be a forgotten demo from those crucial 1978 home recordings that kicked it all off in the first place.

Re-issue of The Durutti Column's seminal 1989 album in its original sleeve. 

‘Vini Reilly’ features the iconic strummer making extensive use of sampling in a style that kept one foot in tradition and another in modernity. The recombinant inventor is a constant in the tremulous top lines, while a phalanx of sampled voices from opera to folk, soul and pop are chopped up in the sampler to ornament his extended lines of melodic thought, encompassing unique takes on classical music and flamenco.

Borne from a difficult period of illness for Vini, one that required him to be wheeled in and out of the studio to meet with engineer/producer Stephen Street, the album is a triumph despite all the rercording difficulties. Opening with a heart-clutching stroke of flamenco and opera in ‘Love No More’ it flows to the stately, waltzing air of ‘Opera I’, and jazz-funk frisson ‘People’s Pleasure Park’, and the diaphanous shape of his sampledelic wonder ‘Finding The Sea’, to a standout in his imagined duet with Otis Redding and Tracy Chapman ‘Otis’, with the breathtaking couplet ‘Requiem Again’ and ‘My Country’ that practically leave you quivering.

items.body:
Sydney's Daily Toll provide a prequel to 2025's 'A Profound Non-Event' here with a selection of demos that highlights their early formative run.

You can always tell the moment you become a bona fide music snob - it's when someone asks you if you like a record and you reply it's good, but not as good as the demos. But sometimes, it's just how it is; Aussie band Daily Toll know the deal and have cracked open their archive, giving the deep listeners an opportunity to watch their sound develop. Recorded between 2021 and 2023, when poet and artist Kata Szász-Komlós and Jasper Craig-Adams were working as a duo, it's a set of eight sweet, roughly recorded sketches that scratch at the core of what made 'A Profound Non-Event' so gripping. 

Never overworked, these songs aren't simple either. 'Preamble' is a slowcore stomper that's fleshed out with evocative environmental recordings, and 'Cherry Tree' is powered by rickety drum machine slaps and jangly Flying Nun-era guitars, while 'U Can't Unhear What's Been Sung' is a Velvet Underground cover band trapped in a humid basement. It's lo-fi gear, but it's not underdeveloped.

items.body:
16 hours of peerless, important works by Eliane Radigue relating to her work with the ARP 2500 synthesiser between 1971-2000. Prior to this period, Eliane worked exclusively with feedback on tape and oscillators, but her work from the ‘70s onward is defined by an uniquely meditative and transcendent grasp of microtonal minimalism which has latterly come to place her among the 20th century’s most esteemed and truly inimitable composers. Bearing in mind that Eliane realised this fathomless body of work in her Paris apartment away from professional recording studios, only makes it resonate more strongly with the idea that Eliane was a genuine outlier whose uniquely sober work divined an unquantifiable yet ultimately human nature in electronic music. RIP legend.

"Eliane Radigue was born in Paris. She studied “musique concrète” techniques at the “Studio d’Essai” of the RTF under the direction of Pierre Schaeffer and Pierre Henry (1956-57). She was married to the painter and sculptor Arman and devoted ten years to their three children. She then worked with Pierre Henry, as his assistant at the Studio APSOME (1967-68). She was in residence at the New York University School of Arts (1970-71), the University of Iowa and the California Institute of the Arts (1973) and Mills College (1998). She has created sound environments using looped tapes of various durations, gradually desynchronising.

Her works have been featured in numerous galleries and museums since the late 60s and from 1970, she has been associated to the ARP 2500 Synthesizer and tape through many compositions from Chry-ptus (1970) up to L’Île resonante (2000). These include: Biogenesis, Arthesis, Ψ 847, Adnos I, II and III (70s), Les Chants de Milarepa and Jetsun Mila (80s) and the three pieces constituting the Trilogie de la Mort (1988-91-93). Since 2002, she has been composing mostly acoustic works for performers and instruments. Her music has been featured in major international festivals. Her extremely sober, almost ascetic concerts, are made of a continuous, ever-changing yet extremely slow stream of sound, whose transformation occurs within the sonic material itself.

Radigue found her musical voice through the decisive encounter with “musique concrète” and its founding fathers. With Pierre Schaeffer, first, and then Pierre Henry, with whom she learned and perfected the art of tape recorders. She then developed a unique style by herself, freely continuing the exploration of electronic sounds, progressing with tenacity through her musical quest, without worrying about current trends or fashions, paying no attention to creeds or dogmas. An isolated course, out with fashions and institutions, such a singular and intense music, so remote from everything..."

items.body:
Numero dust off the wiry, angular new wave of Mikel Rouse’s Tirez Tirez; one time Another Side label mates of Arthur Russell, Parade Ground and Tuxedomoon, and support act for Talking Heads, sharing all of their panache for sophisticated songwriting and pert grooves, at best in the bossa shimmy of ‘Living in This Dream (I’m So Proud)’ and a light-headed title tune...

“Tirez Tirez was founded by Missouri native Mikel Rouse, and gave its first performance as the opening act for the rock band Talking Heads at a 1978 concert in Kansas City, Missouri. The band's initial line-up was Rouse (vocals/guitar), Rob Shepperson (drums) and Jeff Burk (bass). Tirez Tirez issued two very rare self-released LPs in their earliest days: No Double Bagging Necessary (1978) and Rush & Dissonance (1979). All three members of the group subsequently moved to New York City in 1979, and self-released their debut single ("Scattered"/"Scenery") in November of that year. The band's third album (1980's Etudes) was recorded in New York City, but it did not initially see a US release, and was at first only picked up for distribution by the tiny British independent label Object Music. The LP went on to sell a very respectable 2,000 copies in the UK, and US indie Aura Records later issued in the album in the US in late 1981. Aura also issued "Razorblades", a single taken from the album.

Bassist Burk left Tirez Tirez in 1982, and was replaced by James Bergman. Philip Johnston (keyboards/woodwinds) was also added to the group at about the same time. This line-up (Rouse/Shepperson/Bergman/Johnston) recorded 1983's Story Of The Year, which was released only in Europe via Belgian label Les Disques Du Crépuscule. Although he had left Tirez Tirez, original band member Burk would continue to contribute finished artwork to future Tirez Tirez album and single releases after his 1982 departure; the same would be true of original drummer Shepperson after his departure in early 1984.”

The long-awaited sequel to 2013's 'For the World', 'The Final Painting' features guest appearances from Bill Callahan, Sharon Van Etten and Eve Searls.

Ed Askew's been part of New York City's underground since the 1960s, when he released his self-titled debut LP on ESP-Disk. And although he disappeared for decades, just handing out DIY tapes to his closest friends, his re-emergence in 2013 was greeted with global acclaim. But after touring incessantly and sweeping the Euro festival circuit, Askew's health began to decline - he's an octogenarian at this point, so it's to be expected. He took to uploading his new material to Bandcamp, so Jerry David DeCicca, who produced 'For the World' reached out and asked if he could work on a new album with Askew. A few years later, in 2024, they began to work on 'The Final Painting', stitching together studio and home recordings into an intimate, minimal sequel that was finished just before Askew died in January of last year.

The record is a fitting testament not just to Askew's longevity and influence, but his energy even in the final moments of his life. He sounds full of life here, backed by an ensemble who seem to completely understand the rhythm of his lilting poetry. And including Callahan was a masterstroke, if anyone's been informed by Askew's deadpan recollections, it's him.

Masami Akita’s near half century reign of noise terror as Merzbow continues unabated with this new torrent for Barcelona’s Modern Obscure Music

Recorded and mixed at his Munemihouse studio, Tokyo, January 2024, ’Tsubute Mosaic’ yields a white hot flow of psychoactive distortion riddled with the unique pathos that Merzbow brings to J-noise and the wider noise world that he was instrumental in fomenting during the late ‘70s. The famed birder and general advocate for the animal world naturally mimics the chaotic order of things for 37’ cleft in two parts.

Blizzard dynamics shred the senses for the first half of Part 1, before the storm dies down and we appear to move into cave systems populated with thousands of bats, and descend to the depths of hell in its final section. Part 2 sustains buzzsaw revs and squirming electronics in another tempestuous passage of atonality , breaking down into swarms of knife-winged insectoids and bestial squeal that pushes buttons other music doesn’t reach.

Dean Blunt’s totemic, genre-agnostic first ’Black Metal’ album is back in circulation on the heels of its killer 2nd volume, singing out a singular sort of mid-decade London blooz where his myriad circles run into one.

In 2014 ‘Black Metal’ arrived as Blunt’s 4th solo album in a string of quietly groundbreaking and guess-again solo recordings following the break-up of Hype Williams, his duo with Inga Copeland. It was an instant fave, raved about everywhere, and with the benefit of hindsight is arguably one of the past decade’s definitive highlights; a record symptomatic of the way staid generic borders were dissolving, expressing a lucid but woozy pathos that still feels timeless, yet very much of its flat-time, when the stream of musical history had pooled into the reservoir of the internet.

Returning to its slow baked charms years later ‘Black Metal’ has lost none of its allure, with a reflective stillness still belying its depths. Nimbly joining wipe clean presets and crisp licks of original instrumentation with vocals by Blunt and regular spar Joanne Robertson, their baker’s dozen tunes somehow consolidate aspects of everything from hip hop to chamber music, indie-pop to R&B with experimental wit and ohrwurming magick that places it among his most memorable and surprising records.

From the symphonic Americana lilt of ‘Lush’ to its amazing 13 minute centrepiece of chamber soul gauze ‘Forever’ and the free jazz meets folk and roadrap synthscape of ‘Grade’ it coolly piques curiosity and perplexes from every angle, resolving unfamiliar styles with a pop-sharpened manner that follows a path first taken by A.R. Kane and which quite possibly ignited a reappraisal of the problematic way in which Black music has been perceived and categorised in popular/critical culture.

All time business = unmissable.

Porto’s rapidly evolving Perf label go hard on a hip hop-weighted jungle noir flex with local mainstay Spitbender’s debut volley of breakbeat chicanery and dread dub noise tipped FFO UVB-76 Music, Mick Harris, Healing Force Project...

"Always lurking amidst the underground Porto music scene is Spitbender, the most stable moniker of the ever-morphing Francisco Antão. Spin gathers a collection of tracks that demonstrate his experimentalism & coy sonic precision. Spitbender takes cues from Jungle & Hip Hop producers to create his own unique blend of Downtempo. What becomes clear throughout the album is the attention to detail: it is infused as much by Industrial's red-line spectra as it is by the dubplate logic of the Darkside Continuum, yet it does so at its own tripped out speed. 

Spin begins with the laid-back but constantly shifting 'Global Overgroove'. Its breakbeat science moves in & out of DSP glitch-work & dub reflections. When its slinky bassline melody arrives, a certain dread sets in.

'Weyward Fold' drops into a driving, hard-edged chug, threaded with snippets of Malcolm X's disobedient pedagogy. The momentum carries into 'Headnod Doctor', where the bass distortion thickens & the cymbal circuit is overloaded, landing somewhere between Hip‑Hop grit & metal weight.

Side A ends with the downtempo roller 'Dogs and Moles (Skylurk Mix)'. The familiar break drifts into new territory, pulled along & wrapped in a slap-back echo. A quirky melody cuts through the haze, giving the track a fresh tilt. The mulch of the track forms a steady, unhurried pulse.

Spitbender's spacious atmospherics & groove-focused approach comes further into focus on 'Nothing Here But the Recordings'. Creating his own chapter in the book of Trip Hop, his minimalist touch is laid out in full.

'Force the Hand Ov Chance' pulls Boom Bap gently into dub mechanics, letting space do the heavy lifting. Its simplicity hides a deep pocket. 

Returning to broken-up distortion, 'Mirrors of Flesh (Dub Mix)' finds Spitbender using the mixer as an instrument to push & pull the heavy drums of Benjamin Brejon [of Méchanosphere] alongside the voice of Rui intoning the title phrase.

Sitting between the album's two poles, 'Out Take Dub' fuses the clipped‑obsession timbres of Spin's heavier moments with its blissed out flow. Feedback & distortion are welcomed & drawn long.

In the end, Spin hits like a fully formed statement—lean, focused, & unmistakably Spitbender. Every track pushes its own angle, but together they land with a clarity that feels earned. It's a sharp marker in his trajectory, & it leaves a charge in the air."

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

Rose Keeler-Schaffeler's second release 'Universal Language' via Magic Hollow.

"Written and recorded during pregnancy and early motherhood, Rose Keeler-Schaffeler's album draws inspiration from the earliest forms of human communication: coos, cries, sighs and instinctive vocalisations that precede language yet already contain the seeds of music.

Best known as Keel Her, the cult DIY songwriter, producer and NTS Radio DJ whose fiercely independent body of work helped define a generation of bedroom pop, Rose reveals a strikingly different side of her musical practice here. Produced by Daniel O'Sullivan, Universal Language places the human voice at its centre, treating it not as a vehicle for lyrics but as the raw material from which music, language and relationships emerge.

With the exception of a handful of bass vocal parts performed by O'Sullivan, every voice heard on the album is Rose's own.

Across twelve meticulously composed pieces, layered vocal arrangements intertwine with subtle electronics, tape manipulation, synthesizers and understated drum machines. At times the music evokes the luminous purity of medieval sacred music; elsewhere voices dissolve into hazy ambient textures or unfold through hypnotic loops that blur the distinction between singer, choir and atmosphere.

The album was recorded during the first year of her son’s life. Many of its melodic contours and vocal gestures were inspired directly by his earliest sounds. His pre-linguistic attempts at communication became compositional material, guiding Rose towards a deeper exploration of the voice at its point of origin.

Deeply personal yet reaching towards something universal, Universal Language is a meditation on the human voice: our first instrument, our first language and our first experience of belonging."

NWW cruise to Cuba via Cooloorta with Señor Coconut, Andrew Liles, Colin Potter, Matt Waldron & Diarmuid MacDiarmada in tow, on a 2CD expansion of their ludic ’95 LP

Regular cited among NWW’s daftest, most sinisterly whimsical, but also creepy, the original ‘Alice The Goon’ comprised their fruity yet uneasy ’95 homage to Pérez Prado, The King of the Mambo, and a lurid Popeye cartoon, backed with a signature slice of PCP-dosed soundscaping, ‘Prelude to Alice the Goon’ harking to their earliest trips, replete with personnel of that era including David Tibet, Diana Rogerson, and Sarah Dawson, alongside Steven Stapelton and others. 

Both original works are included on this massively expanded 2CD edition, encompassing Diarmuid MacDiarmada’s ‘I Yam What I Yam Intro’ channelling Popeye via Stars on 45 (Pints), and his tripper, 12 min mix ‘And That's All That I Yam Conclusion / Confusion’, plus a standout ‘Coconut Mix’ by Uwe Schmidt’s Señor Coconut, subtly spiced with glitches and hallucinatory electronics for properly uneasy listening. Along with the ’Soliloquy For Lilith’-like drone haunting of ‘Psuedoacacia’, and Matthew Waldron’s crawl-pace, 45’ rabbit hole screw of the ‘Alice the Goon’, it’s a real one for the sky lickers.

Legendary pianist John Tilbury (founding member of free improv titans AMM), captured playing piano, clavichord & organ at home as he approached his 90th birthday this year, ending his recording career with a wonderful, generous set that also includes selected, notable archival works. The set covers everything from Elizabethan songbooks to contemporary compositions by pals including Mark R. Taylor and Catherine Kontz plus archive recordings of pieces by Christian Wolff, Morton Feldman and others, an organ improvisation with Keith Rowe, and much more. As the label perfectly put it - Tilbury is a giant in the history of contemporary, improvised and experimental music -  it’s a real pleasure to have a final document spanning generations, and eras, of his practice. 

From the foreword to the included booklet:

“In 2018 John Tilbury became reluctant to take on more concerts. He lives in Deal on the Kent coast, 80 miles from London, and doesn’t have a car, so, although he was still in demand as a performer, at the age of 82, he decided to end his performing career. When I heard this, I asked whether - if I came to him - he would still be happy to be recorded at home. He said yes, and from then until spring 2026 I travelled to Deal every 6 or 9 months to record John playing piano and clavichord in the lean-to extension at the back of the terrace house where he and his wife Janice live.

We recorded whatever John wanted to play at the time, and so assembled an unusual and varied collection of recordings ranging from pieces from Elizabethan songbooks to new compositions sent by old friends from Scratch Orchestra days. Sometimes, if John was tired or in pain, we didn’t record very much, and the visits became as much a social thing as a recording session - and it was always very enjoyable to talk with John and Janice about music and politics, and hear stories about John’s past and his many musical friends.

In early 2026 – around the time of his 90th birthday - John decided that if we carried on much longer, he’d no longer be able to do justice to the music he was playing, and that we should stop. The original idea – insofar as we had one - was to release a selection of what we’d recorded as an album, but once we started listening back to everything, John suggested that we also include some archive recordings, dating from as far back as the 1970’s. So began a process of discussion, whittling down the many things we could have included, until we agreed on the contents of the four CDs in this box set, which effectively marks the end of John’s recording career.”

Simon Reynell, May 2026

items.body:
Tuareg blues band Amana de Kidal, so named for their north Saharan home town, call for unity between Mali’s myriad ethnicities across a joyful and driving album of pentatonic riffs and rooted grooves.

“Studio album from Bamako-based Tuareg band Amanar de Kidal. "Kel Tamacheq” is years in the making, a self produced DIY album, recorded in the small studios of the Malian capital over the past few years.Carrying on in the tradition of assouf, the Northern Malian style of Tuareg guitar popularized by artists like Tinariwen, Amanar pushes the sound forward into tight upbeat groove and kinetic rhythms, reflecting the rich diversity of Mali and the energy of the capital. 

The band takes its name from their hometown Kidal, a remote outpost deep in the Saharan mountains of the far North. Led by singer/songwriter Ahmed Ag Kaedy, the band Amanar has spent the past 15 years dispersed, with Kaedy making his home in Bamako.

The title, meaning “Tuareg People” in Tamasheq, carries with it a message: a call for unity among the scattered community. Recorded with musicians from across Mali’s many ethnic communities, “Kel Tamasheq” is not just a personal vision, but a sketch for a country at peace. "Among the Tuareg, some are with Mali, some are with the rebels, some are with the Jihadists”, Kaedy says. “The spirit of the album is to say: our misfortune is the source of our division. It's an album driven by Tuareg identity. If we can remember who we are, and let it guide us, we will never lose the road."

Unmissable reissue of Valya Hooi’s standout debut, an immaculately frayed conception of dubwise dream-pop from the same Aussie quarters that gave us HTRK/Jonnine, CS + Kreme, F Ingers...

Valya's first record ‘Untitled’ was originally issued by Altered States Tapes in 2019 (the same year as her song-writing credit on ‘I Don’t Seem Myself Tonight’ from Jonnine’s ’Super Natural’ EP), and has somehow managed to evade our radar until now, when she’s making a fairly big ping in our world.

Working economically with her own vocals, plus guitar, keyboards, and slivers of clarinet supplied by Tarquin Manek (F Ingers, LST), the results can’t help but remind us to aspects of Laila Sakini or Teresa Winter’s music that we hold dearly - namely the reverb-laden vocals and drowsily psychedelic, daydreaming appeal - but also tend toward a sort of sublime, grown-up bedroom chamber darkness understandably shared with her peer Jonnine, and the low-key grooving suss of CS + Kreme, or even Mica Levi at her most strung out. 

An incredible album.

items.body:
Epic 16 hour François Bayle retrospective, an unparalleled document of the key C.20th electro-acoustic and concrète pioneer and director of the hugely influential GRM institution from 1966-1997, where he was instrumental in bringing the Acousmonium speaker array and INA-GRM label to life, among many important, enduring innovations

This 10 year reissue of ’50 Ans d’Acousmagique’ joins INA-GRM’s quintessential boxsets of Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Parmegiani, Radigue, and Xenakis in a rare, stellar microcosm of works by twentieth century groundbreakers. At 16 hrs long, and including 228 tracks, it offers a comprehensive overview of François Bayle’s unfathomable catalogue of work between 1972-2012. During this time Bayle was pivotal in altering perceptions of music’s materiality and purpose at the most fundamental and philosophic levels through his work in developing the Acousmonium diffusion system - an “orchestra of loudspeakers” which has become key to the GRM’s facilities in Paris - as well as supporting technological developments (Syter, GRM Tools, Midi Formers, Acousmographe) which are vital to his own remarkable compositions, and his endeavours organising radio broadcasts and events. 

Deeply informing and paralleling the history of recorded electronic music during its formative golden years, Bayle’s recordings render an embarrassment of riches for the discerning and explorative listener and historians of vanguard C.20th music. Between the flighty electro-acoustic staging of his avian dreams on ’72’s ‘Trois Rêves D'oiseau’ to the sensually lathered cosmic delirium of 1978-80’s ‘Erosphère’ works, to his beguiling latter tributes to his tutors at the Paris Conservatoire and Darmstadt summer courses, Messiaen and Stockhausen; the overwhelming scope of Bayle’s work, and thus the boxset, is brought into clearer focus by its chronological sequencing, offering a logical pathway thru his incredible projections of imagination.

It bears reflection that figures such as François Bayle created, and then opened, doors of perception for music in the past century that have come to mirror and shape the soundsphere we now inhabit. His innovations in sound spatialisation and the embrace of an acoustic unknown, or acousmagique, underline some of the most fascinating expressions of pathos thru art in our lifetimes, and this boxset is more than enough to send heads reeling into deep time for eons to come.

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items.body:
Wiry, tart, cold, minimal wave shrapnel from original early ‘80s upswell of DIY machine music...

“40 years after its creation, MOß GARTEN – Sekvensstyrd 1981–1986 arrives as a compelling double vinyl LP, diving deep into the early Swedish DIY electronic scene. Inspired by pioneers such as Kraftwerk, Cabaret Voltaire, John Foxx, and The Human League, Mikael Isaksson developed a distinct sound situated between minimal electronics, industrial, synth wave, and experimental sound art. At its core was the sequencer: pulsing, programmed structures forming the backbone of dense, often hypnotic compositions.

Working initially with his cousin Jan or friend Thomas and later evolving into a largely one-man project, recordings were made on cassette tapes and in improvised studios—often under time pressure, frequently recorded and mixed within just a few hours. These very limitations gave the tracks their raw and immediate character. Pieces like “Moderna Kvinnor,” “Soon Soon,” “Ensam,” and “Music From The Border” exemplify the uncompromising, sequence-driven (“sekvensstyrd”) approach that defined this era.

Using an arsenal of analog synthesizers, early sequencers, and drum machines, the project created music that feels at once cold, mechanical, and deeply emotional. Sekvenssytrd 1981–1986 is more than a collection of archival recordings—it is a vivid document of a time when electronic music was conceived as a radical and deeply personal form of expression.”
